title: Chapter 9 — The Sermon
paragraphs: Father Mapple rose and in a mild voice of quiet authority ordered the scattered congregation to move together. 'Starboard gangway, there! Move over to port — port gangway to starboard! Midships! Midships!'
There was a low rumbling of heavy sea boots among the benches and an even slighter shuffling of women's shoes, and then all was quiet again, every eye on the preacher.

He paused a moment, then kneeled in the bow of the pulpit, folded his large brown hands across his chest, raised his closed eyes, and offered a prayer so deeply reverent that he seemed to be kneeling and praying at the bottom of the sea.

When he finished, in prolonged, solemn tones — like the continuous tolling of a bell on a ship foundering at sea in fog — he began reading the following hymn. But as he reached the final stanzas, his manner changed, and he burst forth with pealing joy and exultation:
'The ribs and terrors in the whale / Arched over me a dismal gloom, / While all God's sunlit waves rolled by, / And lifted me deepening down to doom.
'I saw the opening maw of hell, / With endless pains and sorrows there; / Which none but they that feel can tell — / Oh, I was plunging to despair.
'In black distress, I called my God, / When I could scarce believe him mine, / He bowed his ear to my complaints — / No more the whale did me confine.
'With speed he flew to my relief, / As on a radiant dolphin borne; / Awful, yet bright, as lightning shone / The face of my Deliverer God.
'My song forever shall record / That terrible, that joyful hour; / I give the glory to my God, / His all the mercy and the power.'

Nearly everyone joined in singing this hymn, which swelled high above the howling storm. A brief pause followed. The preacher slowly turned the pages of the Bible and at last, pressing his hand down on the right page, said: 'Beloved shipmates, hold tight to the last verse of the first chapter of Jonah: "And God had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah."'

'Shipmates, this book — just four chapters, four yarns — is one of the smallest strands in the mighty cable of Scripture. Yet what depths of the soul does Jonah's deep sea-line plumb! What a powerful lesson this prophet teaches us! What a magnificent canticle from the fish's belly! How surging and grandly it billows! We feel the floods washing over us; we sink with him to the kelp-covered bottom; seaweed and all the slime of the sea is around us! But what is this lesson that the book of Jonah teaches? Shipmates, it's a two-stranded lesson: a lesson to us all as sinful men, and a lesson to me as a pilot of the living God. As sinful men, it's a story of sin, hard-heartedness, sudden fear, swift punishment, repentance, prayer, and finally deliverance and joy. Like all sinners, Jonah's sin was willful disobedience of God's command — never mind what the command was or how it was delivered — a command he found hard. But everything God wants us to do is hard for us — remember that — which is why he more often commands than persuades. And if we obey God, we must disobey ourselves; and it's in this disobeying of ourselves that the hardness of obeying God consists.'

'With this sin of disobedience in him, Jonah further defies God by trying to flee from Him. He thinks a man-made ship can carry him to countries where God doesn't rule — where only the captains of this earth hold power. He skulks around the wharves of Joppa, looking for a ship bound for Tarshish. And there may be a deeper meaning here. By all accounts, Tarshish was the modern Cadiz. And where is Cadiz, shipmates? Cadiz is in Spain — as far by water from Joppa as Jonah could possibly have sailed in those ancient days, when the Atlantic was an almost unknown sea. Joppa — modern Jaffa — sits on the easternmost coast of the Mediterranean, and Tarshish is more than two thousand miles to the west, just outside the Straits of Gibraltar. Don't you see, shipmates? Jonah tried to flee as far from God as the world allowed! Miserable man! Skulking from his God with a slouched hat and guilty eyes, prowling among the shipping like a burglar rushing to cross the seas. He looks so disordered and self-condemning that if there had been police in those days, he'd have been arrested on suspicion before he touched a deck. He's obviously a fugitive — no luggage, no hat-box, no bag — no friends seeing him off at the wharf. After much dodging around, he finds the Tarshish ship loading its last cargo. As he steps aboard to find the captain's cabin, all the sailors stop hoisting goods to study the stranger's guilty eyes. Jonah sees this and tries in vain to look confident — tries his wretched smile. But strong instinct tells the sailors he's no innocent man. In their half-joking, half-serious way, one whispers to another: "Jack, he's robbed a widow." "Joe, mark him — he's a bigamist." "Harry, I bet he's that adulterer who broke jail in Gomorrah, or one of the missing murderers from Sodom." Another runs to read the wanted poster nailed to the wharf, offering five hundred gold coins for a parricide. He reads, looks from Jonah to the poster. All the sailors crowd around Jonah, ready to seize him. Frightened Jonah trembles, and trying to put on a brave face, only looks more cowardly. He won't confess — but that itself deepens suspicion. He makes the best of it, and when they decide he's not the wanted man, they let him pass. He goes below to the cabin.'

'"Who's there?" cries the captain at his busy desk, hurriedly filling out customs papers. "Who's there?" Oh, how that harmless question torments Jonah! For an instant he almost turns to flee again. But he rallies. "I want passage to Tarshish. How soon do you sail, sir?" The busy captain hadn't even looked up, but the moment he hears that hollow voice, he shoots Jonah a piercing glance. "We sail with the next tide," he says slowly, still studying him intently. "No sooner?" "Soon enough for any honest man traveling as a passenger." Ha! Jonah — another stab. But he quickly distracts the captain from that scent. "I'll sail with you — the passage money, how much? I'll pay now." Because it's specifically noted, shipmates, as if it were a detail not to be overlooked, that "he paid the fare" before the ship sailed. And in context, this is full of meaning.'

'Now Jonah's captain, shipmates, was a man whose judgment could detect crime in anyone, but whose greed would expose it only in the penniless. In this world, sin that pays its way travels freely, without a passport, while Virtue, if poor, is stopped at every border. So the captain tests the depth of Jonah's purse before judging him openly. He charges triple the normal fare — and Jonah agrees. Now the captain knows Jonah is a fugitive, but he's willing to assist a flight that paves its trail with gold. Yet when Jonah actually opens his purse, the captain's suspicions persist. He tests every coin for counterfeits. "Not a forger, anyway," he mutters, and books Jonah's passage. "Show me my room, sir," says Jonah. "I'm weary from traveling. I need sleep." "You look it," says the captain. "There's your room." Jonah enters and tries to lock the door, but there's no key. Hearing him fumble, the captain laughs quietly and mutters something about convicts' cell doors never being locked from inside. Fully dressed and dusty, Jonah throws himself into his berth, finding the ceiling almost touching his forehead. The air is stifling, and Jonah gasps. In that cramped hole, sunk below the ship's waterline, Jonah feels a foreshadowing of that suffocating hour when the whale will hold him in the tightest chamber of its belly.'

'Screwed to the wall, a swinging lamp rocks gently in Jonah's room. The ship heels toward the wharf under the weight of the last cargo, and the lamp, flame and all, though swaying, maintains a constant angle to the room — perfectly straight itself, but making obvious the crooked, lying levels around it. The lamp terrifies Jonah. Lying in his berth, his tormented eyes scan the room, and this so-far-successful fugitive finds no rest for his restless gaze. The lamp's contradiction appalls him more and more. The floor, ceiling, and walls are all askew. "Oh! So my conscience hangs in me!" he groans. "Straight upward it burns, but the chambers of my soul are all twisted!"'

'Like a man who after a night of drunken revelry staggers to bed, still reeling, but with conscience pricking him — who turns and turns in agony, praying for oblivion until the episode passes — and at last, amid the whirl of suffering, a deep stupor steals over him, like the numbness of bleeding to death, for conscience is the wound and nothing can stanch it — so, after sore wrestling in his berth, Jonah's ponderous misery drags him drowning down to sleep.'

'Now the tide has turned. The ship casts off, and from the deserted wharf the cheerless vessel for Tarshish glides to sea, all leaning to one side. That ship, my friends, was the first recorded smuggler! The contraband was Jonah. But the sea rebels — it will not bear the wicked burden. A terrible storm comes on; the ship is about to break apart. But when the boatswain calls all hands to lighten her, when boxes, bales, and jars are clattering overboard, when the wind is shrieking and the men are shouting and every plank thunders with trampling feet right over Jonah's head — in all this raging chaos, Jonah sleeps his horrible sleep. He sees no black sky, feels no reeling timbers, barely notices the rush of the mighty whale already cleaving the seas after him with open mouth. Yes, shipmates, Jonah had gone down into the sides of the ship and was fast asleep. But the terrified captain comes and screams in his deaf ear: "What do you mean, sleeper? Arise!" Startled from his stupor, Jonah staggers to his feet, stumbles to the deck, and grabs a rope to look out at the sea. But at that moment a panther-wave leaps over the bulwarks and pounces on him. Wave after wave floods the ship; the sailors nearly drown while still afloat. And whenever the pale moon shows her frightened face through steep canyons in the black sky overhead, Jonah sees the bowsprit rearing skyward, then plunging back down toward the tormented deep.'

'Terrors upon terrors run screaming through his soul. In all his cringing postures, the God-fugitive is now unmistakable. The sailors watch him. Their suspicions grow, and finally, to test the truth by referring the matter to Heaven itself, they cast lots to discover whose fault this tempest is. The lot falls on Jonah. Then how furiously they mob him with questions: "What is your occupation? Where are you from? What country? What people?" But mark, shipmates, the behavior of poor Jonah. The eager sailors only ask who he is and where he's from. But they receive not only an answer to those questions — they get an answer to a question they never asked, an unsolicited confession forced from Jonah by the hard hand of God upon him.'

'"I am a Hebrew," he cries — and then: "I fear the Lord God of Heaven, who made the sea and the dry land!" Fear Him, Jonah? Yes, well might you fear the Lord God then! He goes on to make a full confession, and the sailors grow more and more appalled — but still they pity him. When wretched Jonah, not yet asking God for mercy because he knows all too well the darkness of what he deserves, cries out for them to throw him into the sea, knowing the storm is his fault — they mercifully turn away and try other means to save the ship. But it's no use. The furious gale howls louder. Then, with one hand raised to God in prayer, with the other they reluctantly take hold of Jonah.'

'And now Jonah is taken up like an anchor and dropped into the sea. Instantly, an oily calm spreads from the east, and the sea goes still — as if Jonah carried the gale down with him, leaving smooth water behind. He sinks into the whirling heart of such a masterless chaos that he barely notices the moment he drops, seething, into the yawning jaws waiting for him. The whale snaps shut all its ivory teeth like white bolts upon his prison. Then Jonah prayed to the Lord from the fish's belly. But notice his prayer, and learn a weighty lesson. Sinful as he is, Jonah does not weep and beg for immediate rescue. He feels his terrible punishment is just. He leaves all deliverance to God, contenting himself with this: that despite all his agony, he will still look toward God's holy temple. And here, shipmates, is true and faithful repentance — not clamoring for pardon, but grateful for punishment. And how pleasing to God this was is shown in Jonah's eventual deliverance from the sea and the whale. Shipmates, I don't hold up Jonah as a model of sin, but I do hold him up as a model of repentance. Don't sin — but if you do, repent like Jonah.'

While he spoke these words, the howling, slanting storm outside seemed to add new power to the preacher. Describing Jonah's storm, he seemed tossed by a storm himself. His deep chest heaved like a ground swell; his arms seemed the warring elements at work; and the thunder rolling from his dark brow and the light leaping from his eyes made every simple listener watch him with a strange, quick fear.
Then a lull came over his expression as he silently turned the pages of the Book once more. At last, standing motionless with closed eyes, he seemed for a moment to be communing with God and himself.
But again he leaned toward the congregation, and bowing his head with an expression of the deepest yet manliest humility, he spoke these words:

'Shipmates, God has laid only one hand upon you; both His hands press upon me. I have read you, by whatever murky light is mine, the lesson Jonah teaches to all sinners — and therefore to you, and even more to me, for I am a greater sinner than you. And now how gladly I would come down from this masthead and sit on the hatches where you sit, and listen as you listen, while one of you reads me that other, more terrible lesson that Jonah teaches to me as a pilot of the living God. How, being an anointed pilot-prophet, a speaker of truth, and commanded by the Lord to sound unwelcome truths in the ears of wicked Nineveh, Jonah — dreading the hostility he would provoke — fled from his mission and tried to escape his duty and his God by taking ship at Joppa. But God is everywhere; Tarshish he never reached. As we have seen, God came upon him in the whale and swallowed him down to living gulfs of doom, tearing him along "into the midst of the seas," where the swirling depths sucked him ten thousand fathoms down and "the weeds were wrapped about his head" and all the watery world of misery poured over him. Yet even then, beyond the reach of any plumb line — "out of the belly of hell" — when the whale grounded on the ocean's deepest bones, even then God heard the engulfed, repenting prophet when he cried. Then God spoke to the fish, and from the shuddering cold and blackness of the sea, the whale rose breaching toward the warm, pleasant sun and all the delights of air and earth, and "vomited out Jonah upon the dry land." And when the word of the Lord came a second time, Jonah — bruised and beaten, his ears still echoing with the ocean like two sea shells — did the Almighty's bidding. And what was that, shipmates? To preach the Truth to the face of Falsehood! That was it!'

'This, shipmates, is that other lesson — and woe to the pilot of the living God who ignores it. Woe to him whom this world charms away from Gospel duty! Woe to him who tries to pour oil on the waters when God has brewed them into a gale! Woe to him who seeks to please rather than to shake! Woe to him whose reputation means more to him than righteousness! Woe to him who, in this world, doesn't court dishonor! Woe to him who would not be true, even though being false would save him! Yes, woe to him who, as the great Pilot Paul said, while preaching to others is himself a castaway!'

He sank and fell away from himself for a moment. Then lifting his face again, a deep joy shone in his eyes as he cried out with heavenly passion: 'But oh! Shipmates! On the starboard side of every woe, there is a sure delight — and the peak of that delight is higher than the depth of that woe is deep. Isn't the masthead higher than the keel is low? Delight is to him — a far, far upward and inward delight — who against the proud gods and commodores of this earth, stands forever forth as his own inexorable self. Delight is to him whose strong arms still support him when the ship of this base, treacherous world has gone down beneath him. Delight is to him who gives no quarter to the truth, and kills, burns, and destroys all sin, though he pluck it from under the robes of senators and judges. Delight — topgallant delight — is to him who acknowledges no law or lord but the Lord his God, and is only a patriot to heaven. Delight is to him whom all the waves of the billows of the seas of the raging mob can never shake from this sure Keel of the Ages. And eternal delight and blessedness will be his, who coming to lay himself down, can say with his final breath — O Father! — chiefly known to me by Thy rod — mortal or immortal, here I die. I have striven to be Thine, more than to be this world's, or my own. Yet this is nothing; I leave eternity to Thee; for what is man that he should live out the lifetime of his God?'
He said no more. Slowly waving a benediction, he covered his face with his hands and remained kneeling until every person had left and he was alone in the place.
